source_text: CAPUT OCTAVUM, De Dei absoluta exsistendi necessitate. Hactenus de attributis Dei, quae sunt loco proprietatum, essentiam ipsius consequentium in genere: nunc de singulis seorsim ac discretim dicturis occurrit prae caeteris I. Absoluta exsistendi necessitas, quae est ea Dei perfectio, per quam is ita est seu exsistit, ut non possit non esse. Sacrae literae hoc attributum immortalitatis & incorruptibilitatis nominibus indigitant, 1 Tim. 6.16.17; Rom. 1.23. Dicitur perfectio Dei pro negationis istius, qua necessitatem hanc declaramus, fundamento, quod est positiva perfectio, in Deo revera exsistens, quae materialiter, ut vulgo loquuntur, per hoc attributum significatur. Formalis autem ratio illius posita est in negatione alicujus imperfectionis, quae communiter omnibus creaturis inest, & contingentiae vocatur.
english: CHAPTER EIGHT. On God's absolute necessity of existing.

Thus far concerning the attributes of God which stand in place of properties consequent upon His essence in general: now, about to speak of the several ones separately and distinctly, there occurs before the rest I. Absolute necessity of existing, which is that perfection of God by which He so is or exists that He cannot not be.

The sacred letters point out this attribute by the names of immortality and incorruptibility (1 Timothy 6:16-17; Romans 1:23). It is called a perfection of God for the foundation of that negation by which we declare this necessity, which foundation is a positive perfection really existing in God, which materially, as they commonly speak, is signified by this attribute. But its formal ratio is placed in the negation of some imperfection which commonly inheres in all creatures and is called contingency.

source_text: Major duobus modis probatur. Primo, quia ens independens vel exsistens a seipso, exsistit vi essentiae sive naturae suae, ac proinde illi exsistentia tam necessario competit, quam essentia. Secundo, quia ens independens, nec potuit aliquando non fuisse, nec posthac non esse. Ergo est absolute necessarium. QUARTO, Confessione etiam gentilium philosophorum. Orpheus enim dixit rerum omnium necessitatem, hoc est, substantiam, quae sit necessario per seipsam, & a qua caetera omnia dependeant, ipsa vero a nullo. Aristoteles: Deum dicit, ens necessarium, perpetuum. Apulejus: necessitatem ipsam nihil aliud, quam Deum, dici censuerim. Avicenna: Illud sanctum esse ens necessarium, quod ex se est, non vero entia reliqua, etiamsi ab alio habeant necessitatem exsistendi.
english: The major is proved in two ways. First, because an independent being or one existing from itself exists by the force of its essence or nature, and therefore existence belongs to it as necessarily as essence. Second, because an independent being neither could once not have been, nor hereafter not be. Therefore it is absolutely necessary.

FOURTH, also by the confession of Gentile philosophers. For Orpheus spoke of the necessity of all things — that is, a substance which is necessarily through itself, and on which all the rest depend, but itself on none. Aristotle calls God a necessary, perpetual being. Apuleius: I would judge necessity itself to be called nothing other than God. Avicenna: That holy thing is the necessary being which is from itself, but not the remaining beings, even if they have necessity of existing from another.

source_text: Errat vero, qui putat, hoc attributum, vel ad immutabilitatem, vel ad aeternitatem revocari debere. Quemadmodum enim res mutari proprie non est eas vel produci, ut sint, vel destrui, ut non sint: sed salva exsistentia aliquid formaliter acquirere vel amittere. Ita contra immutabilem esse, non est idem atque non posse non esse; sed proprie significat, non posse novam perfectionem acquirere, vel aliqua privari, salva manente exsistentia. Ex quibus colligitur, non parum differre necessitatem exsistendi & immutabilitatem; cum haec mutabilitati, illa contingentiae opponatur. Est autem huic necessitati aeternitas propinquior, etsi in hoc differant, quod haec durationis principium & finem, illa vero contingentiam sive potentiam non exsistendi negat: ideoque, ut immutabilitas aeternitatis quaedam, qua causa est & ratio prior, ita haec necessitas aeternitatis. Atque ita, Deum aeternum esse, hoc est, durationis suae principio & fine carere, conficimus ex hoc, quod ipse est ens necessarium, cui non esse omnino adversatur.
english: But he errs who thinks this attribute ought to be reduced either to immutability or to eternity. For just as for things to be changed properly is not for them either to be produced so that they are, or to be destroyed so that they are not, but with existence remaining safe to acquire or lose something formally — so conversely to be immutable is not the same as not to be able not to be; but properly signifies not to be able to acquire a new perfection, or to be deprived of any, with existence remaining safe.

From which it is gathered that necessity of existing and immutability differ not a little; since this is opposed to mutability, that to contingency. But eternity is nearer to this necessity, although they differ in this, that this denies the beginning and end of duration, but that denies contingency or the power of not existing: and therefore, as immutability is a certain [cause] of eternity, of which it is the prior cause and reason, so this necessity [is a cause] of eternity. And so we conclude that God is eternal — that is, lacks beginning and end of His duration — from this, that He Himself is a necessary being, to whom not to be is altogether adverse.

source_text: Asserimus autem hanc absolutam exsistendi necessitatem ita propriam esse Deo, ut nulli creaturae attribui possit. Quamvis enim nonnulla entia creata dicantur necessaria, ut substantiae spirituales & corpora caelestia: ea tamen non simpliciter, sed secundum quid ita appellantur; quia naturaliter & vi causarum naturalium destrui nequeunt; id quod proprie loquendo est esse incorruptibile.
english: But we assert that this absolute necessity of existing is so proper to God that it can be attributed to no creature. For although some created beings are called necessary, as spiritual substances and heavenly bodies: yet they are so called not simply but in a certain respect; because they cannot be destroyed naturally and by the force of natural causes — which properly speaking is to be incorruptible.

source_text: DEMONSTRAMUS autem Deum esse ens absolute necessarium, PRIMO, sacrae Scripturae testimoniis, 1 Tim. 6.16.17; Rom. 1.23; Psal. 102.27.28, ubi Deus immortalis & incorruptibilis dicitur ac rebus corruptibilibus opponitur, semperque permanere statuitur ad declarandam absolutam exsistendi necessitatem. Unde & Augustinus lib. 1. de Trin. cap. 1: Cum, inquit, anima quodammodo immortalis esse dicatur, non diceret Apostolus, Qui solus habet immortalitatem, nisi quia vera immortalitas incommutabilitas est, quam nulla habere potest creatura, quoniam solius creatoris est. SECUNDO, Nomine Dei, Eheje, Exod. 3.14. quo absoluta exsistendi necessitas indicatur, ut testatur Nazianzenus Orat. 24. sive 2. de theol. & August. lib. de vera relig. cap. 49. Hacpropter Deus etiam sibi soli ipsum esse attribuit, tanquam qui solus sit necessario, Esai. 42.8; Amos 5.8. TERTIO, ratione. Omne enim ens independens, atque quod a se exsistit, est absolute necessarium. Deus est ens independens, exsistens nimirum a seipso, ut demonstratum est cap. 2. de Dei exsistentia. Ergo Deus est ens absolute necessarium.
english: But we demonstrate that God is an absolutely necessary being, FIRST, by the testimonies of sacred Scripture (1 Timothy 6:16-17; Romans 1:23; Psalm 102:27-28), where God is called immortal and incorruptible and is opposed to corruptible things, and is established always to remain, to declare absolute necessity of existing. From which also Augustine (On the Trinity 1.1): Although, he says, the soul is said to be immortal in a manner, the Apostle would not say, Who alone has immortality, unless because true immortality is incommutability, which no creature can have, since it belongs to the Creator alone.

SECOND, by the Name of God, Eheje (Exodus 3:14), by which absolute necessity of existing is indicated, as Nazianzen (Oration 24 / 2 on theology) and Augustine (On True Religion, chapter 49) testify. For this reason God also attributes Being to Himself alone, as He who alone is necessarily (Isaiah 42:8; Amos 5:8).

THIRD, by reason. For every independent being, and what exists from itself, is absolutely necessary. God is an independent being, existing namely from Himself, as was demonstrated in chapter 2 on God's existence. Therefore God is an absolutely necessary being.
